hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Discord's Cassandra message schema partitioned by (channel_id, bucket), where bucket is a fixed time window. Why add the bucket?
options: To let Cassandra sort messages alphabetically
To bound partition size, so a busy, long-lived channel doesn't grow one partition forever
To spread a single message across several nodes
To enable cross-channel joins
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: With channel_id alone, an active channel's partition would grow without limit, and huge partitions hurt Cassandra reads and compaction. Discord's 2017 post describes a static ~10-day bucket in the partition key, with message_id as the clustering key. Cassandra has no joins.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: According to Discord's 2017 engineering post, why did they move message storage off MongoDB?
options: MongoDB couldn't store Unicode emoji
MongoDB had no replication
The data and indexes no longer fit in RAM, and latencies became unpredictable
Licensing costs became too high
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Discord began with a single MongoDB replica set. As messages grew into the billions, the working set outgrew memory and latency became erratic, so they chose Cassandra for scalable, predictable write-heavy storage. Replication and Unicode weren't the issues.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Which problems did Discord's 2023 post cite with their large Cassandra cluster?
options: Hot partitions, JVM garbage-collection pauses and compaction backlogs causing latency spikes and on-call toil
Lack of secondary indexes and SQL joins
Inability to replicate across datacenters
Message IDs colliding across channels
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Busy channels concentrated reads on single partitions, GC pauses caused latency spikes, and compaction falling behind made reads worse. Operators spent a lot of time nursing the cluster. Multi-DC replication is a Cassandra strength, and Snowflake IDs don't collide.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Discord placed Rust 'data services' between the API and the database. What key technique did they use to protect hot partitions?
options: Caching every message in Redis permanently
Batching writes into daily files
Rejecting reads for channels with more than 1,000 members
Request coalescing: concurrent identical reads share a single database query
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: When a big announcement goes out, thousands of clients request the same channel's messages at once. Coalescing collapses them into one DB query whose result is fanned back out. Routing by channel (consistent hashing) sends those requests to the same instance so coalescing works.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Why was ScyllaDB attractive to Discord as a Cassandra replacement?
options: It's a document database with flexible schemas
It's written in C++ with no garbage collector, uses a shard-per-core design, and is compatible with Cassandra's query language and drivers
It provides strict serializable transactions across all rows
It stores data only in memory
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Scylla reimplements Cassandra's data model and CQL in C++ (Seastar), so there are no JVM GC pauses, and each core owns a shard. Discord could keep its data model while getting more predictable latency. It is a wide-column store, not a document DB or an in-memory one.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: In Cassandra-style stores, a channel where users deleted millions of messages becomes very slow to read. Why?
options: Deleted rows are moved to a separate slow table
Deletes trigger a full cluster repair on every read
Deletes write tombstones, and reads must scan past them until compaction purges them after the grace period
Deleted data is decrypted on every read
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: A delete is a write of a tombstone marker. Reads that cross a range full of tombstones must process them all, which costs CPU, memory and GC, until compaction drops them after gc_grace_seconds. Discord's 2017 post describes hitting exactly this.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Discord uses Snowflake-style message IDs as the clustering key. What does that buy them?
options: IDs are time-ordered, so sorting by message_id gives chronological order without a separate timestamp sort
IDs are encrypted, so message content stays private
IDs guarantee no two channels ever have messages in the same millisecond
IDs can be guessed by clients, which avoids an extra round trip
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Snowflake IDs put a timestamp in the high bits, so clustering on message_id stores messages chronologically within a partition and 'latest N messages' is a cheap ordered slice. Encryption and uniqueness across channels aren't what the ordering provides.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: Which outcomes did Discord report after migrating messages from Cassandra to ScyllaDB? Select all that apply.
options: The cluster went from 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes
p99 read latency became lower and much more stable
All writes moved to strongly consistent Paxos transactions
Messages were moved into PostgreSQL
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Discord's 2023 post reports 177 to 72 nodes, and p99 reads dropping from roughly 40–125 ms to about 15 ms. The data stayed in a Cassandra-compatible wide-column store with the same consistency model. There was no Paxos-everywhere change and no move to Postgres.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: How did Discord's data-service layer reduce load on hot message partitions? Select all that apply.
options: Requests for the same channel were routed to the same data-service instance via consistent hashing
Concurrent identical reads were coalesced into one database query
A single channel's messages were scattered randomly across all nodes
Clients were made to poll less often by increasing app timeouts
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: Channel-affinity routing concentrates duplicate requests where they can be merged, and coalescing merges them. Randomly scattering a channel would break range reads, and the fix was server-side, not a client polling change.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: ScyllaDB is a JVM-based fork of Cassandra that relies on a carefully tuned garbage collector for low latency.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: False. ScyllaDB is a C++ reimplementation built on the Seastar framework. It has no JVM or GC, which is a major reason Discord saw steadier tail latency than with Cassandra.

hld-bigtech-cases:0.prompt: In Discord's Cassandra message store, a user editing a message while another deletes it could leave a row holding only the primary key and the edited text, so Discord had to detect and clean up such rows.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:0.explanation: True. Every Cassandra write is an upsert resolved last-write-wins per column, so the edit re-created the text column after the delete. Writing the whole message on edit could resurrect deleted messages, so Discord instead treated a null author_id (a required column) as corrupt and deleted the row ('How Discord Stores Billions of Messages', 2017).

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: What does Netflix's Chaos Monkey do?
options: Load-tests services with synthetic traffic in staging
Randomly terminates production instances so teams must build services that tolerate instance loss
Injects bugs into code before deployment
Shuts down whole AWS regions every day
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: Chaos Monkey kills instances during business hours, so instance failure becomes routine and services must be stateless and redundant. Region-level evacuation tests are Chaos Kong, a separate and much rarer exercise.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: How does Netflix Open Connect get content onto its edge appliances?
options: It fetches each title from AWS the first time a subscriber requests it
Subscribers' devices share segments peer-to-peer
It proactively pre-positions content during off-peak hours, based on predicted popularity in each location
ISPs upload titles themselves from DVDs
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: Netflix knows its catalog and can forecast demand, so Open Connect Appliances are filled overnight during a 'fill window', when ISP links are quiet. Peak-hour streaming then comes from local disk instead of cache misses, unlike a pull-through CDN.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Why are ISPs willing to host Netflix Open Connect Appliances in their networks?
options: Netflix provides the appliances at no charge, and serving locally cuts the ISP's upstream transit traffic
ISPs earn a fee per gigabyte streamed
Regulators require it
The appliances also serve as the ISP's DNS resolvers
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: Netflix ships OCAs to qualifying ISPs for free. Because a large share of evening traffic is Netflix, serving it inside the ISP saves expensive transit and improves quality for subscribers, which benefits both sides.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: When a Netflix member opens the app, browses and presses Play, which part is served from AWS and which from Open Connect?
options: Everything is served from AWS
Everything is served from Open Connect
Browsing comes from Open Connect and video from AWS
Browsing, recommendations, auth and playback steering run in AWS; video bytes come from Open Connect appliances
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: The control plane (UI APIs, personalization, licensing, choosing which OCAs to use) lives in AWS. Once playback starts, the client streams from OCA URLs it was given. This separates the compute-heavy logic from the bandwidth-heavy delivery.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: What problem was Netflix's Hystrix library designed to solve in its microservice architecture?
options: Service discovery
Cascading failures: it wrapped remote calls with timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks
Distributed tracing of requests
Encrypting traffic between services
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: A slow dependency can exhaust a caller's threads and spread the outage. Hystrix isolated each dependency, failed fast when its circuit opened, and served fallbacks. Discovery was Eureka's job. Hystrix has been in maintenance mode since 2018, and the patterns live on in libraries like Resilience4j.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: What does Netflix's Chaos Kong exercise validate?
options: That a single container can restart cleanly
That database backups can be restored
That traffic can be evacuated from an entire AWS region to the remaining regions without a major member impact
That new code passes unit tests
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: Netflix runs active-active across multiple AWS regions. Chaos Kong simulates losing a whole region and shifts its traffic to the others, proving capacity and failover work before a real regional outage. Instance-level failure is Chaos Monkey's domain.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Which event Netflix has publicly described pushed it to move from its own datacenter to AWS?
options: A major database corruption in 2008 that stopped it from shipping DVDs for three days
A DDoS attack on its streaming launch day
A fire in its primary datacenter
An AWS sales promotion
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: The 2008 corruption showed the risk of vertically scaled single points of failure. Netflix chose horizontally scalable, distributed systems in the cloud and completed the migration in early 2016.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Match Netflix OSS components to their roles. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Eureka: service discovery registry
Zuul: edge gateway/router for incoming requests
Hystrix: latency and fault tolerance (circuit breakers)
Chaos Monkey: load balancer for streaming traffic
Kafka: created at Netflix for chaos experiments
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: Eureka, Zuul and Hystrix were core Netflix OSS pieces. Chaos Monkey kills instances rather than balancing load, and Kafka was created at LinkedIn (Netflix uses it heavily for its data pipeline).

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Why does Netflix run chaos experiments in production instead of only in staging? Select all that apply.
options: Staging can't faithfully reproduce real traffic, data, configuration and dependency behavior
It builds confidence that the actual system people use tolerates failure
Production experiments need no blast-radius controls because failures never reach members
Netflix runs no pre-production testing at all
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: The principle is to experiment on the real system, since that's where emergent failures hide. Netflix still limits blast radius carefully (ChAP routes only a small share of traffic into experiments) and still does pre-production testing.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Netflix serves the majority of its streaming video bytes directly from AWS EC2 instances.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: False. Video is served from Netflix's own Open Connect CDN appliances in ISPs and internet exchanges. AWS hosts the control plane: APIs, personalization, encoding pipelines and steering.

hld-bigtech-cases:1.prompt: Netflix's Chaos Automation Platform (ChAP) limits blast radius by routing a small slice of traffic into a control group and an experiment group and comparing their metrics.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:1.explanation: True. ChAP injects failures (e.g. latency or errors from a dependency) only for the experiment cohort and stops automatically if key metrics such as stream starts degrade. That makes production chaos safe enough to run continuously.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Your server's POST /v1/payment_intents call to Stripe times out and you don't know whether it succeeded. What does Stripe recommend?
options: Retry the same request with the same Idempotency-Key header
Retry with a new Idempotency-Key so it's treated as fresh
List recent payments and guess which one is yours
Never retry payment calls
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Reusing the key makes the retry safe: if the first attempt went through, Stripe returns the saved result instead of creating a second payment. A new key would create a duplicate.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: You retry a Stripe request using the same idempotency key but change the amount. What happens?
options: Stripe processes the new amount and replaces the old result
Stripe silently returns the original result
Stripe returns an error because the parameters don't match the original request for that key
Stripe creates a second object linked to the first
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Stripe's idempotency layer compares incoming parameters with the original request and errors on a mismatch, which protects against accidental key reuse. Silently returning the original would hide a client bug.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Per Stripe's docs, the first request with an idempotency key started executing and returned a 500 error. You retry with the same key. What do you get?
options: A fresh attempt that may succeed
The same saved 500 result
A 409 telling you to use a new key
A 404 because failed requests aren't stored
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request that began executing, whether it succeeded or failed, including 500s, and replays them. Results aren't saved when the request failed validation or conflicted with a concurrent request, so those can be retried with the same key.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: How should a Stripe client generate idempotency keys?
options: Use the current Unix timestamp in seconds
Use the customer's email address
Use an incrementing integer that resets on deploy
Generate a random V4 UUID (or similarly high-entropy value) per logical operation, and reuse it for that operation's retries
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Stripe suggests V4 UUIDs or other random strings with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Timestamps and counters collide across processes or after restarts, and an email would merge unrelated payments for the same customer.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: How does Stripe's date-based API versioning work for an account?
options: The account is pinned to the API version current at its first request; upgrades are opt-in, and a Stripe-Version header can override per request
Every account is upgraded automatically on each release
Clients must send a version in the URL path, such as /v37/charges
Old versions are switched off every month
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Stripe pins each account to a dated version (e.g. 2024-06-20) and internally transforms responses back to older shapes, so breaking changes never surprise existing integrations. The '/v1' in URLs is a stable prefix, not the evolving version.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Stripe's guidance on network retries is to use exponential backoff with jitter. Why the jitter?
options: It makes requests harder to fingerprint
It's required by TLS
It spreads retries from many clients over time so they don't hit the server in synchronized waves
It shortens the total time to give up
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: After an incident, clients that all failed at the same moment would retry at the same moments under pure exponential backoff, so their retries arrive together in bursts. Random jitter desynchronizes them and lets the service recover.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Stripe list endpoints paginate with `starting_after=<object id>` instead of page numbers or offsets. Why?
options: Offsets aren't supported by HTTP
Cursors are stable when new objects are inserted and don't require skipping N rows on every page
Object IDs are smaller than integers
It lets clients jump to any random page
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: With offsets, inserts shift items between pages (causing duplicates or gaps), and deep offsets get slower. Keying on the last seen ID is stable and index-friendly. Random page jumps are exactly what cursors give up.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Which statements match Stripe's documented idempotency behavior? Select all that apply.
options: Keys may be removed automatically once they are at least 24 hours old
Sending a key on GET or DELETE has no effect, since those are already idempotent
No result is saved if the request failed validation before the endpoint began executing
Keys never expire, so a key from last year still replays its result
Stripe generates the key and returns it in the first response
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Those three come straight from Stripe's docs. Keys can be pruned after 24 hours, so they're meant for retry windows rather than permanent deduplication, and the client generates the key so it exists before the first attempt.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Stripe object IDs carry type prefixes such as `cus_`, `pi_` and `ch_`. What are the benefits? Select all that apply.
options: Humans can tell the object type at a glance in logs and support tickets
The API can return a clearer error when an ID of the wrong type is passed
The prefix encodes the account's secret key
The prefix guarantees global ordering across object types
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: Stripe has written about prefixed IDs as a developer-experience feature: they're self-describing for debugging and make wrong-type mistakes easy to spot. They carry no secrets and impose no ordering.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: With Stripe, a second request using the same idempotency key while the first is still executing is rejected rather than executed a second time.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: True. Stripe returns an idempotency error for a concurrent request with an in-use key, and saves no result for it, so the client can retry later and get the original outcome. This closes the race a simple check-then-insert would leave open.

hld-bigtech-cases:2.prompt: Stripe's versioning requires every client to send the newest version header, and old versions stop working with each release.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:2.explanation: False. Accounts stay pinned to their version until they choose to upgrade. Stripe maintains backward-compatibility transforms so integrations written years ago keep working.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Uber open-sourced H3, a hexagonal hierarchical spatial index. What is the main advantage of hexagons for its marketplace analysis?
options: Hexagons nest perfectly inside larger hexagons
All six neighbors share an edge and are equidistant from the center, which makes neighbor and gradient analysis uniform
Hexagons need no special handling anywhere on the globe
Hexagon IDs are human-readable street addresses
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: Squares have neighbors at two different distances (edge versus corner), and triangles at three. Hexagons have one, which simplifies smoothing and k-ring aggregation for supply, demand and pricing. H3 children only approximately nest, and 12 pentagons per resolution need special handling.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Uber's Ringpop, used in its Node.js dispatch services, provided what capability?
options: A geospatial index built on quadtrees
Real-time map tile rendering
A message queue replacing Kafka
Application-layer sharding via consistent hashing, with SWIM-based gossip for cluster membership
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: Ringpop let a cluster of Node.js processes agree on membership (SWIM gossip) and route each key, such as a geo cell or rider, to its owner on a hash ring, forwarding requests when needed. It wasn't a spatial index or a queue.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: In Uber's 2015 talks on its dispatch system, which spatial library was described for dividing the map into cells to shard supply?
options: Google's S2 geometry library
PostGIS R-trees
Elasticsearch geo_point
Geohash strings in MySQL
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: The dispatch rewrite talks describe using S2 cells (from projecting the sphere onto a cube) as shard keys for supply. H3 came later and became Uber's open-source standard for hexagonal analysis such as pricing.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: In H3, how does a cell relate to the next finer resolution?
options: Each cell is split into exactly 4 children that tile it perfectly
Each cell has about 7 children (aperture 7) that only approximately cover the parent
Each cell has 32 children, like geohash
Resolutions are independent with no parent/child relationship
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: H3 uses aperture 7: each hexagon has about 7 children, each with roughly one-seventh of the area. Because hexagons can't be divided exactly into smaller hexagons, children only approximately fill the parent. Four children is quadtree or S2 behavior, and 32 is geohash.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Why use consistent hashing (as Ringpop does) rather than `hash(key) % N` to assign cells to dispatch nodes?
options: It guarantees a perfectly even load
It needs no hash function
When a node joins or leaves, only about 1/N of keys move instead of almost all of them
It keeps keys sorted by geography
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: With modulo, changing N remaps nearly every key and causes a storm of state movement. A hash ring moves only the keys adjacent to the changed node. Even load still needs virtual nodes, and hashing doesn't preserve geographic order.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Why does representing an H3 cell as a 64-bit integer matter for large-scale data pipelines?
options: It makes cells compact, fast-to-compare keys for joins, group-bys and hash partitioning
It encrypts location data
It means only 64 cells exist
It makes cells exactly equal in area
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: An H3 index packs resolution and cell digits into one 64-bit value, so 'aggregate trips per hexagon' becomes a cheap integer group-by or join. It isn't encryption, there are billions of cells at fine resolutions, and areas vary slightly.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Uber has described using H3 to bucket supply and demand for dynamic pricing. Why bucket by hexagon instead of raw GPS points?
options: GPS points can't be stored in databases
Pricing must be identical across a whole city
Hexagons hide all location data from the pricing team
Aggregating into cells gives stable local counts to compare supply against demand and to smooth across neighbors
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: Pricing needs per-area ratios, such as open requests versus idle drivers. Discrete cells turn noisy point data into counts that can be computed, cached and smoothed over k-rings. The point is local variation, not city-wide uniformity.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Which statements about H3 are true? Select all that apply.
options: It has 16 resolutions (0 through 15)
Each resolution includes exactly 12 pentagons
A cell index fits in a 64-bit integer
Child cells nest perfectly inside their parent
It uses square cells for simpler math
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: H3 projects onto an icosahedron, giving 16 resolutions with 12 pentagons each (topology requires them), and indexes fit in 64 bits. Hexagons can't be split exactly into smaller hexagons, so nesting is approximate, and the cells are hexagons by design.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: Ringpop used the SWIM protocol for membership. Which properties make SWIM suitable for large clusters? Select all that apply.
options: Failure detection doesn't depend on a central coordinator
Each node probes only a few random peers per period, so message load per node stays roughly constant as the cluster grows
Membership changes spread epidemically by piggybacking on probe messages
Every node always has an identical, strongly consistent view of membership
It requires a ZooKeeper ensemble to run
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: SWIM's randomized probing, indirect pings and gossip dissemination scale well with no central service. The trade-off is that membership views are only eventually consistent, so nodes can briefly disagree, which is why it doesn't need ZooKeeper.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: H3 was created and open-sourced by Uber.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: True. Uber open-sourced H3 in 2018. It's now widely used beyond Uber for geospatial analytics, with bindings in many languages and support in several databases.

hld-bigtech-cases:3.prompt: A grid can tile the whole sphere using only hexagons at every resolution, so H3 contains no other cell shapes.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:3.explanation: False. A sphere can't be tiled by hexagons alone. H3 places 12 pentagons at each resolution (at the icosahedron's vertices, mostly over oceans), and code doing neighbor traversal must handle them.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Instagram's 2012 'Sharding & IDs' post describes a 64-bit ID layout. What is it?
options: 32 bits timestamp, 32 bits random
41 bits timestamp, 10 bits machine ID, 12 bits sequence
41 bits milliseconds since a custom epoch, 13 bits logical shard ID, 10 bits per-shard sequence
64 bits from a central auto-increment counter
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: Instagram's IDs are 41 bits of time, 13 bits of logical shard (up to 8,192) and 10 bits of sequence. The 41/10/12 split is Twitter Snowflake's (timestamp, worker, sequence), the most common confusion.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Why did Instagram want IDs that sort roughly by creation time?
options: So 'newest first' queries can sort or range-scan on the primary key without a separate timestamp index
So IDs are easier to memorize
Because PostgreSQL requires sorted primary keys
To hide how many photos exist
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: Feeds and profiles are time-ordered, so time-prefixed IDs make ORDER BY id DESC equivalent to newest-first and keep inserts at the right edge of the B-tree. Postgres doesn't require sorted keys, and time-prefixed IDs actually reveal timing.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Instagram created thousands of logical shards mapped onto far fewer physical database servers. What does that design enable?
options: Cross-shard joins in a single SQL query
Avoiding any routing logic in the application
Making each logical shard exactly the same size
Rebalancing by moving whole logical shards to new machines, without rehashing data or changing IDs
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: A shard's ID never changes, only the logical-to-physical mapping. When a server fills up, some logical shards (PostgreSQL schemas) move to a new server. Picking a large logical count up front avoids painful resharding later. Joins across shards still aren't possible.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: With Instagram's 10-bit per-shard sequence, how many IDs can one logical shard generate in a single millisecond?
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: 10 bits give 2^10 = 1,024 values per shard per millisecond (the sequence is taken mod 1024). 4,096 is Snowflake's 12-bit sequence, and 8,192 is Instagram's 13-bit shard space.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys a poor fit for a write-heavy, time-ordered table in a B-tree database?
options: UUIDs can collide frequently
Databases cannot index 128-bit values
Random values insert all over the index, causing page splits and poor cache locality, and they don't sort by time
UUIDs must be generated by a central server
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: Random keys land on random leaf pages, so the working set is the whole index and inserts fragment it. They're also twice the size of a 64-bit ID and give no time ordering. Collisions are vanishingly rare, and UUIDs are generated anywhere.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Given Instagram's layout (41-bit time | 13-bit shard | 10-bit sequence), which expression extracts the shard ID from a BigInt id?
options: (id >> 10n) & 0x1FFFn
id & 0x3FFn
id >> 23n
(id >> 13n) & 0x3FFn
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: Shift right by 10 to drop the sequence, then mask 13 bits (0x1FFF = 8191) to remove the timestamp. `id & 0x3FF` is the sequence, and `id >> 23n` is the timestamp. Embedding the shard lets any service route by ID with no lookup table.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Facebook's TAO (USENIX ATC 2013) serves the social graph. Which description fits it?
options: A strongly consistent SQL database replacing MySQL
A geographically distributed, read-optimized caching layer over sharded MySQL that exposes objects and associations
A message queue for news feed fan-out
A key-value store for photos and videos
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: TAO models the graph as objects (nodes) and associations (typed edges), caches them in tiers of leader and follower caches, and persists to sharded MySQL. It favors read throughput with eventual consistency across regions. Photos live in blob storage (Haystack, f4).

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Which statements about Snowflake-style time-prefixed 64-bit IDs are true? Select all that apply.
options: If a server's clock moves backwards, the generator can produce duplicate or out-of-order IDs unless it guards against it
A 41-bit millisecond timestamp covers roughly 69 years from the chosen epoch
IDs from different shards or workers are strictly increasing across the whole system
Each ID needs a round trip to a central coordinator
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: 2^41 ms ≈ 2.2 trillion ms ≈ 69.7 years, and clock regressions are a known hazard (generators wait or refuse to issue IDs). Ordering across generators is only approximate (k-sorted), and the whole point is generating IDs locally without coordination.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Which drawbacks did Instagram cite for the ID-generation alternatives it rejected? Select all that apply.
options: UUIDs are 128 bits and don't sort naturally by time
Snowflake added moving parts: running a separate ID service plus ZooKeeper
Flickr-style ticket databases add a dedicated write path that can become a bottleneck
PostgreSQL had no way to run logic that generates IDs inside the database
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: Instagram considered UUIDs, Snowflake and ticket DBs, then generated IDs inside PostgreSQL itself using a PL/pgSQL function per shard schema. So Postgres could clearly do it, which is the scheme they shipped.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: In Instagram's design, each logical shard was implemented as a PostgreSQL schema.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: True. Each logical shard was a Postgres schema containing the sharded tables and its own ID-generation function. Moving a schema to another physical server rebalances data without changing any IDs.

hld-bigtech-cases:4.prompt: Instagram's 2012 scheme generated IDs in a separate application service that the web tier called before each insert.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:4.explanation: False. IDs were generated inside each PostgreSQL shard by a PL/pgSQL function used as the column default. Avoiding a separate ID service was a deliberate goal.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: WhatsApp famously handled huge numbers of connections per server with a small team. Which runtime underpinned its chat servers?
options: Node.js on Linux
Erlang on the BEAM VM (running on FreeBSD)
Go with goroutines
Java with Netty
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: WhatsApp built on Erlang (originally on an ejabberd/XMPP foundation) on FreeBSD. BEAM's lightweight processes, one per connection, plus heavy OS tuning enabled millions of connections per box.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: In Slack's real-time messaging architecture (2023 engineering post), what is the split between Gateway Servers and Channel Servers?
options: Gateway Servers store messages, and Channel Servers render the UI
Both are stateless HTTP API servers
Gateway Servers hold client WebSocket connections and subscribe to channels, while Channel Servers own channels (via consistent hashing) and fan messages out to subscribed gateways
Channel Servers hold WebSockets, and Gateway Servers write to MySQL
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: Gateways are the connection tier near users. Each channel is owned by one Channel Server on a consistent-hash ring, which pushes new messages to every gateway that has subscribers for that channel. Messages are persisted through the web API and database, not by these servers.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: Why did Slack build Flannel, an application-level edge cache?
options: Booting a client in a large team required a huge payload of every user and channel; Flannel let clients lazy-load only the data they needed
To cache images and file uploads
To replace MySQL as the system of record
To provide end-to-end encryption
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: Slack's original rtm.start returned the whole team's users and channels, which grew enormous for big organizations. Flannel sits near clients, holds team metadata and serves it on demand, cutting connect time and load on the backend.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: Slack originally sharded MySQL by workspace. Per its post on adopting Vitess, what was the main problem?
options: MySQL couldn't store emoji reactions
Workspaces were too small to shard
Sharding forced every query to fan out to all shards
Very large enterprise workspaces outgrew a single shard and created hot spots, and finer-grained keys like channel were needed
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: Per-workspace shards were simple, but one huge customer could saturate a shard. Vitess let Slack shard by other keys (e.g. channel ID) while keeping MySQL. The issue was too-coarse tenancy, not fan-out.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: A chat app must not lose messages when a recipient's phone is offline. Which delivery design fits?
options: Deliver only to currently connected clients and drop the rest
Store-and-forward: persist the message server-side, push it when the device reconnects, and remove or mark it once the client acknowledges
Ask the sender to resend every few minutes until it works
Broadcast to all devices globally and let them filter
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: The server keeps undelivered messages and uses client acks (with message IDs for dedup on retry) to know when delivery happened. WhatsApp documents that messages are deleted from its servers once delivered. Dropping or relying on sender retries loses messages.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: A message is posted to a channel with 50,000 members. How do architectures like Slack's fan it out efficiently?
options: Insert one row per member into a per-user inbox table before replying
Send it once to the channel's owner server, which pushes one copy per subscribed gateway; each gateway delivers to its local connections
Have every member poll the channel every second
Email each member
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: Fan-out happens in memory over the connection tier: one hop to the channel owner, one per gateway, then local sockets. The message is stored once. Per-member inbox writes (fan-out-on-write) would mean 50,000 DB writes per message.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: WhatsApp's messages are 'deleted from our servers once delivered'. Which property does that store-and-forward model rely on?
options: The server must permanently archive chat history for search
Recipients must be online when the message is sent
The server needs a reliable delivery acknowledgment from the recipient's device before it discards the message
Messages are sent peer-to-peer without servers
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: The server is a transient relay: it holds the message until the recipient's device confirms receipt, then drops it. History lives on devices (and optional user backups). Without reliable acks, deleting would lose messages.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: Which presence (online/away) designs scale to millions of users? Select all that apply.
options: Heartbeats that refresh a TTL, so a missed heartbeat expires the user to offline
Sending presence updates only to clients that are currently viewing or subscribed to that user
Broadcasting every presence change to every user in a huge workspace
Writing every heartbeat to the primary relational database
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: TTL-based liveness avoids explicit logout handling, and interest-based subscription keeps fan-out proportional to what users actually see. Broadcasting is O(N²) traffic in big orgs, and persisting heartbeats floods the DB with throwaway writes.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: How do chat systems typically give users a consistent message order within a conversation? Select all that apply.
options: A single owner per channel assigns increasing sequence numbers or server timestamps
Clients order by that server-assigned value and can detect gaps to request missing messages
Every message across all channels globally is placed in one total order
Clients trust their own device clocks for ordering
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: Per-conversation ordering from a single owner is cheap and is all users can perceive. Sequence numbers also make gaps detectable after reconnects. Global total order is unnecessary and costly, and device clocks drift.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: WhatsApp engineers publicly reported more than 2 million concurrent TCP connections on a single server in 2012.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: True. WhatsApp's January 2012 blog post ('1 million is so 2011') reported over 2 million connections on one FreeBSD server running Erlang, after kernel and BEAM tuning.

hld-bigtech-cases:5.prompt: With end-to-end encryption, the chat server can still read message contents to build server-side search indexes.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:5.explanation: False. In E2EE (e.g. WhatsApp's Signal Protocol, rolled out in 2016) only endpoints hold the keys, and the server relays ciphertext. Search must happen on-device, which is a real product trade-off.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: In Shopify's pods architecture, what is a pod?
options: A Kubernetes pod running one Rails process
A group of microservices owned by one team
A CDN edge location
A fully isolated set of datastores (e.g. MySQL, Redis, Memcached) that holds a subset of shops
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Shopify partitions by shop: each shop lives in exactly one pod, and the pod has its own datastores. The name has nothing to do with Kubernetes pods, a common confusion in interviews.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Why do pods help Shopify survive flash sales (e.g. a celebrity product drop)?
options: A hot shop can only saturate its own pod's datastores, so merchants in other pods are unaffected
Pods automatically give each shop unlimited database capacity
Pods cache every checkout page at the CDN
Pods queue all writes until the sale ends
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Pods limit blast radius: noisy-neighbor effects from one merchant's spike stay inside one pod. A single shop's write capacity is still bounded by its pod, which is why checkout throttling exists too.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: A request for `some-shop.myshopify.com` arrives. How does Shopify get it to the correct pod's data?
options: Every pod receives every request and ignores the ones it doesn't own
DNS returns a different IP per pod and clients cache it forever
Software in the load balancers (Shopify calls it Sorting Hat) matches the request to its pod, adds a header and forwards it; app servers use that header to talk only to that pod's datastores
The shop ID is hashed modulo the number of pods on every request
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Shopify's pods post (2018) describes Sorting Hat matching every request to a pod with a list of rules, tagging it with a header and forwarding it. App servers are shared, but each request touches only one pod's datastores. An explicit shop-to-pod mapping, unlike hashing by pod count, lets shops move between pods; broadcasting would break isolation.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: One pod becomes overloaded because a few shops grew huge. How does Shopify rebalance?
options: Split each shop's tables across several pods
Rehash every shop to a new pod count
Ask merchants to export and re-import their data
Move individual shops to another pod online, using a binlog-based migration tool (Ghostferry) with a brief cutover
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Shopify open-sourced Ghostferry, which copies a shop's rows and tails the MySQL binlog to keep them in sync, then performs a short cutover and updates the routing table. Shops are the unit of movement and never split across pods.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Since a shop's data never spans pods, what is the main cost of the pod model?
options: Single-shop queries become distributed transactions
Queries spanning many shops (platform-wide analytics, reporting) can't run against one database and go to separate data pipelines or warehouses
Every request needs two-phase commit
Shops can't have more than one product
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Tenant-based partitioning makes in-shop work local and transactional, but cross-tenant queries need a separate system that aggregates data from all pods. Single-shop queries are the easy case.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Shopify's core commerce application is well known for which architectural choice?
options: Thousands of independently deployed microservices from day one
A large Ruby on Rails modular monolith with enforced component boundaries
A serverless architecture built entirely on functions
A Java EE application server cluster
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Shopify has written extensively about deconstructing its monolith into components inside one Rails codebase (tooling such as Packwerk enforces boundaries) rather than splitting into microservices. Pods scale the data layer beneath that app.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: During a flash sale, checkout requests for one shop exceed what its pod's database can handle. What is the right protective pattern?
options: Throttle or queue checkouts at the edge and admit buyers at a rate the pod can sustain
Let all requests through and rely on database autoscaling
Temporarily move the shop into every pod at once
Disable inventory checks so writes are cheaper
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Admission control in front of checkout (Shopify has written about scriptable load balancers for this) keeps the pod healthy and gives buyers a fair queue. Databases don't scale up instantly, and skipping inventory checks causes overselling.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Which are genuine properties or trade-offs of Shopify's pods? Select all that apply.
options: A failure or overload in one pod has a limited blast radius
Capacity grows by adding more pods
A single very hot shop is still bounded by its one pod's capacity
A single shop's writes automatically scale across all pods
Pods remove the need for any request routing
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Isolation and horizontal growth are the benefits, and the per-shop ceiling is the inherent limit, mitigated by throttling and moving big shops to roomier pods. Shops don't span pods, and routing to the right pod is essential.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Compared with sharding every table by a hash of its row ID, why is partitioning by tenant (shop) a good fit for Shopify? Select all that apply.
options: All of one shop's data is colocated, so joins and transactions within a shop stay local
Uneven tenant sizes mean big shops may need moving to keep pods balanced
Most requests touch only one shop, so they hit a single pod
Every request must fan out to all pods to find a shop's rows
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: Commerce requests are naturally scoped to a shop, so tenant colocation keeps them on one pod with local transactions. The flip side is skew between tenants. Fan-out would happen with row-hash sharding, not tenant-based routing.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: In Shopify's pods model, one shop's data is deliberately split across several pods to spread its load.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: False. A shop lives entirely in one pod. That keeps queries and transactions local and makes isolation possible. Rebalancing moves whole shops rather than splitting them.

hld-bigtech-cases:6.prompt: Shopify's pods are an instance of cell-based architecture: self-contained units that each serve a subset of customers and contain failures.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:6.explanation: True. Cells (pods) partition customers into independent units with their own data stores, behind a thin routing layer. The same pattern appears at AWS and Slack as a way to cap blast radius and scale by adding cells.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: What was Discord primarily optimizing for in its Cassandra → ScyllaDB migration?
options: Stronger transactional consistency for messages
Cheaper object storage for attachments
Predictable tail latency and less operational toil at trillions of messages
Supporting SQL joins across channels
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: GC pauses, hot partitions and compaction pain drove the move. The data model and consistency stayed essentially the same. The gain was steadier p99s and far fewer firefights, with fewer nodes.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: What were Netflix's main goals in building Open Connect rather than relying only on commercial CDNs?
options: Lower delivery cost and better streaming quality by serving video from inside ISP networks
Stronger DRM for its content
Hosting its recommendation engine
Avoiding AWS for its control plane
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: At Netflix's traffic share, an owned CDN with predictive overnight fill and placement inside ISPs cuts transit costs and keeps bitrates high at peak. DRM and recommendations aren't delivery problems, and the control plane stayed in AWS.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Stripe's idempotency-key design optimizes first and foremost for:
options: Minimizing API latency
Correctness under retries: a network failure should never cause a double charge
Reducing storage costs
Letting clients skip authentication on retries
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Payments can't tolerate duplicates, and networks fail ambiguously. Idempotency keys make retries safe, which matters far more than a little extra latency or storage. Authentication is still required on every request.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Instagram's 2012 ID scheme optimized for which combination?
options: Human-readable IDs and alphabetical sorting
Strict global monotonicity and a single coordinator
Encryption and anonymity of creation time
Time-sortable 64-bit IDs generated inside the existing database, with no new service to operate
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: With a small team, Instagram wanted no extra moving parts. Generating Snowflake-like IDs in PostgreSQL per shard gave sortability and shard routing without running ZooKeeper or an ID service. Global strict ordering was explicitly not required.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: In an HLD interview you mention Shopify's pods. What makes that reference strong rather than name-dropping?
options: Reciting the exact number of pods Shopify runs
Claiming the design must copy Shopify exactly
Naming the constraint (spiky, tenant-scoped load and noisy neighbors), explaining how pods address it, and saying whether your system shares that constraint
Mentioning as many companies as possible in one answer
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Interviewers want reasoning: what problem forced the design, what it costs (no cross-tenant queries, per-tenant ceilings), and whether it fits the problem in front of you. Trivia and copying signal pattern-matching without understanding.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Which pairing of company and primary bottleneck it designed around is correct?
options: Discord: payment double-charges; Stripe: chat fan-out
Netflix: bandwidth delivery at peak; Uber: real-time geospatial matching of supply and demand
Shopify: video transcoding; Instagram: driver dispatch
Slack: ID generation; Netflix: ledger reconciliation
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Netflix's dominant cost and quality driver is moving video bytes at peak, and Uber's is matching moving drivers to riders in real time. The other pairings swap companies with problems that belong to someone else.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Discord's request coalescing, Netflix's off-peak pre-positioning and CDN origin shields share which underlying idea?
options: Using strong consistency everywhere
Writing every request synchronously to the system of record
Replacing caches with bigger databases
Removing duplicate or ill-timed work from the hot path before it reaches the scarce resource
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Each technique protects a bottleneck (DB partition, peak-hour links, origin) by merging identical requests or moving work to a cheaper time or tier. They're about load shaping, not consistency or bigger databases.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Which of these are primarily techniques for limiting blast radius? Select all that apply.
options: Shopify's pods (shop-level cells)
Netflix's multi-region setup validated by Chaos Kong evacuations
Circuit breakers and bulkheads as in Netflix's Hystrix
Instagram's time-sortable IDs
Stripe's date-based API versioning
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Cells, regional failover and dependency isolation all contain failures. Time-sortable IDs solve ordering and sharding, and API versioning protects integrations from breaking changes rather than isolating runtime failures.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Which are examples of a company building its own infrastructure because off-the-shelf options didn't fit its scale or problem? Select all that apply.
options: Netflix building the Open Connect CDN
Uber creating the H3 hexagonal index
Discord writing Rust data services in front of its database
Instagram writing a new database engine to replace PostgreSQL
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: Netflix, Uber and Discord each built bespoke components for a specific bottleneck. Instagram did the opposite: it kept PostgreSQL and added sharding and ID generation on top, which is a good example of choosing boring technology.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: The lesson of Discord's move to ScyllaDB is that Cassandra is a bad choice for any chat system.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: False. Cassandra served Discord well from billions to trillions of messages. Its JVM-related latency and operational costs only became decisive at that scale. Case studies teach context-dependent trade-offs, not universal verdicts.

hld-bigtech-cases:7.prompt: Instagram (PostgreSQL), Shopify (MySQL) and Slack (MySQL via Vitess) all kept a relational database as their system of record and scaled it by sharding rather than replacing it.
options: True
False
hld-bigtech-cases:7.explanation: True. Each kept relational guarantees and mature tooling and added partitioning (logical shards, pods, Vitess keyspaces) on top. It's a recurring pattern: shard what you know before adopting something exotic.
